First, load data site northern France. , use provided data (ocsge_metaleurop roi_metaleurop) along ggplot2 package visualization.  vector polygons, define habitats species. habitat combination favorable, unfavorable, neutral zones. geometries rasterized (converted regular grids) prepare modeling.  habitat specificities included project. Currently, 935 species, including 499 birds, 215 mammals, 136 reptiles, 85 amphibians. example, common vole (Microtus arvalis):  … greater white-toothed shrew (Crocidura russula):  understand 3 maps detail, please refer Habitat page. Briefly: Global weight: carrying capacity (general attractiveness) environment species. Foraging weight: trophic attractiveness environment. animal necessarily feed everywhere lives. Resistance (Movement resistance / Spatial friction): energetic cost danger associated crossing environment. parameter used connectivity dispersal models (like Omniscape algorithm discussed later). stage, now habitats defined, rasterize habitats based default layer, cd_ground. allows us landscape grid can successfully overlay layers.
code: # Load a study area (e.g., the Metaleurop site) and its land cover data data("roi_metaleurop") data("ocsge_metaleurop")  ggplot() +   theme_minimal() +   geom_sf(data=ocsge_metaleurop, aes(fill=code_cs), color=NA) +   geom_sf(data=roi_metaleurop, fill=NA, color="red", size=1) +   theme(legend.position = "none") +   labs(title="Land Cover in the Region of Interest (ROI)") # Example: Loading a background concentration raster for a contaminant (Cadmium) ground_cd <- load_raster_extdata("ground_concentration_cd_compressed.tif")  # Habitat definition based on OSGE codes (which are in the `ocsge_metaleurop` table) layer_soil_natural = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%    c("CS1.2.1","CS2.1.1.1","CS2.1.1.2","CS2.1.1.3", "CS2.1.2","CS2.1.3","CS2.2.1","CS2.2.3") layer_soil_artificial = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%   c("CS1.1.1.1", "CS1.1.1.2", "CS1.1.2.1") layer_plant = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%     c("CS2.1.1.1", "CS2.1.1.2", "CS2.1.1.3", "CS2.1.3", "CS2.2.1") habitat_sol = habitat() |>   add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_natural,]) |>   add_nohabitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_artificial,]) plot(habitat_sol) habitat_plante = habitat() |>   add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_plant,]) |>   add_nohabitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_artificial,]) microtus_hab <- join_ocsge_species(ocsge_metaleurop, "Microtus_arvalis") plot_species_habitat(microtus_hab) crocidura_hab <- join_ocsge_species(ocsge_metaleurop, "Crocidura") plot_species_habitat(crocidura_hab) # We use the `weight_global` as habitat habitat_herbivore <- habitat(microtus_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=microtus_hab$weight_global) |>   add_nohabitat(microtus_hab[microtus_hab$resistance==10,]) habitat_carnivore <- habitat(crocidura_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=crocidura_hab$weight_global) |>   add_nohabitat(crocidura_hab[crocidura_hab$resistance==10,]) # We initialize habitat grids (rasters) for each level rast_sol <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_sol) rast_plant <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_plante) rast_herbivor <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_herbivore) rast_carnivor <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_carnivore)  # We create the `raster_stack` of the habitats stack_habitat <- raster_stack(   raster_list = list(rast_sol, rast_plant, rast_herbivor, rast_carnivor),   names = c("soil", "plant", "herbivore", "carnivore") )  terra::plot(stack_habitat)

title: Getting Started: Overview of spacemodR
text: Animals static. individual’s exposure depends movements (foraging radius, dispersal). spacemodR allows simulate movements, instance via convolution kernels circuit theory (Omniscape).
code: # Compute dispersal kernels based on a mobility radius (e.g., in pixels) k_herb <- compute_kernel(radius=50, GSD=25, size_std=0.5) k_carn <- compute_kernel(radius=150, GSD=25, size_std=0.5)  # Apply dispersal to the spacemodel spcmdl_dispersal <- spcmdl |>   dispersal("herbivore", method="convolution", method_option=list(kernel=k_herb)) |>   dispersal("carnivore", method="convolution", method_option=list(kernel=k_carn))  # Note: In this example, the soil and plants are static and do not disperse.

title: Getting Started: Overview of spacemodR
text: Now system set , can “inject” actual pollutant concentrations soil, model bioconcentration bioaccumulation top food chain using transfer() function.
code: # 1. Assign the actual concentration grid into the "soil" layer spcmdl_dispersal[["soil"]][] <- ground_cd  # 2. Define the transfer equations (Bioaccumulation / Bioconcentration Factors) fluxes <- flux(spcmdl_dispersal, default = 1) |>   add_flux("soil", "plant",  ~ 10^x / 32) |> # Specific equation for plants   add_flux("soil", "herbivore",  0.5) |>     # Simple transfer factor for the herbivore   add_flux("herbivore", "carnivore",  0.8)   # Simple transfer factor for the carnivore  # 3. Gather our dispersal kernels for the exposure calculation kernels <- list(soil = NA, plant = NA, herbivore = k_herb, carnivore = k_carn)  # 4. Compute the global transfer throughout the ecosystem spcmdl_transfer <- transfer(spcmdl_dispersal, kernels, fluxes)  # Visualize the contamination absorbed by the carnivore color_transfer <- colorRampPalette(c("white", "#A33D0A"))(255) terra::plot(spcmdl_transfer, col=color_transfer)

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Tout commence par la géographie. spacemodR facilite l’extraction et la manipulation de données d’occupation du sol (comme la base OCS-GE en France) pour une zone d’intérêt (Region Interest - ROI). Nous chargeons dans un premier temps les données d’un site dans le nord de la France. Ici, utilise les présente (ocsge_metaleurop et roi_metaleurop) ainsi que le package ggplot2 pour la représentation.  À partir de ces polygones, nous définissons des habitats pour nos espèces. Un habitat est une combinaison de zones favorables, défavorables ou neutres. Ces géométries sont ensuite transformées en grilles régulières (rasters) prêtes pour la modélisation.  Certaines de ces spécificités d’habitats sont incluses dans le projet. Pour l’instant, 935 espèces dont 499 oiseaux, 215 mammifères, 136 reptiles et 85 amphibiens. Par exemple pour le campagnol des champs (Microtus arvalis):  … et la musaraigne grise commune (Crocidura russula):  Pour comprendre les 3 cartes en détails, ce référer à la page Habitat. Brièvement: Global weight (pondération globale), c’est la capacité d’accueil (ou l’attractivité générale) d’un milieu pour l’espèce. Foraging weight (pondération de recherche de nourriture) : c’est l’attractivité trophique du milieu. Un animal ne se nourrit pas forcément partout où il vit. Resistance (résistance au déplacement / Friction spatiale) : c’est le coût énergétique ou le danger lié à la traversée de ce milieu. Ce paramètre est utilisé par les modèles de connectivité et de dispersion (comme l’algorithme Omniscape abordé plus tard). cette étape, maintenant que les habitats sont défini, rasterize les habitats selon une couche par défaut, ici cd_ground, qui va permettre d’avoir la même grille paysagère afin de pouvoir superposer toutes les couches.
code: # Charger une zone d'étude (ex: site de Metaleurop) et les données d'occupation du sol data("roi_metaleurop") data("ocsge_metaleurop")  ggplot() +   theme_minimal() +   geom_sf(data=ocsge_metaleurop, aes(fill=code_cs), color=NA) +   geom_sf(data=roi_metaleurop, fill=NA, color="red", size=1) +   theme(legend.position = "none") +   labs(title="Occupation du sol sur la zone d'étude") # Exemple: Chargement d'un raster de la concentration de fond d'un contaminant (Cadmium) ground_cd <- load_raster_extdata("ground_concentration_cd_compressed.tif")  # Définition d'habitat à partir des code OSGE (qui sont dans le tableau `ocsge_metaleurop`) layer_soil_natural = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%    c("CS1.2.1","CS2.1.1.1","CS2.1.1.2","CS2.1.1.3", "CS2.1.2","CS2.1.3","CS2.2.1","CS2.2.3") layer_soil_artificial = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%   c("CS1.1.1.1", "CS1.1.1.2", "CS1.1.2.1") layer_plant = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%     c("CS2.1.1.1", "CS2.1.1.2", "CS2.1.1.3", "CS2.1.3", "CS2.2.1") habitat_sol = habitat() |>   add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_natural,]) |>   add_nohabitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_artificial,]) plot(habitat_sol) habitat_plante = habitat() |>   add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_plant,]) |>   add_nohabitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_artificial,]) microtus_hab <- join_ocsge_species(ocsge_metaleurop, "Microtus_arvalis") plot_species_habitat(microtus_hab) crocidura_hab <- join_ocsge_species(ocsge_metaleurop, "Crocidura") plot_species_habitat(crocidura_hab) # nous utilise le poids `weight_global` comme habitat habitat_herbivore <- habitat(microtus_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=microtus_hab$weight_global) |>   add_nohabitat(microtus_hab[microtus_hab$resistance==10,]) habitat_carnivore <- habitat(crocidura_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=crocidura_hab$weight_global) |>   add_nohabitat(crocidura_hab[crocidura_hab$resistance==10,]) # On initialise des grilles d'habitats (raster) pour chaque maillon rast_sol <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_sol) rast_plant <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_plante) rast_herbivor <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_herbivore) rast_carnivor <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_carnivore)  # On créé le `raster_stack` des habiats stack_habitat <- raster_stack(   raster_list = list(rast_sol, rast_plant, rast_herbivor, rast_carnivor),   names = c("sol", "plante", "herbivore", "carnivore") )  terra::plot(stack_habitat)

text: Une fois nos cartes créées, nous devons relier ces couches par des interactions écologiques. spacemodR utilise un Graphe Orienté Acyclique (DAG) pour définir les proies, les prédateurs, et le flux de l’énergie (ou des contaminants).
code: # Construction du réseau trophique trophic_df <- trophic() |>   add_link(from = "sol", to = "plante") |>   add_link(from = "plante", to = "herbivore") |>   add_link(from = "herbivore", to = "carnivore")  # Visualisation des liens trophiques plot(trophic_df)

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Le spacemodel est le cœur du package. Il lie intrinsèquement la dimension spatiale (le raster_stack) et la dimension écologique (le graphe trophic_df). Toute opération ultérieure (dispersion, exposition) utilisera cet objet pour garantir la cohérence des calculs.
code: spcmdl <- spacemodel(stack_habitat, trophic_df) print(spcmdl) #> class       : SpatRaster #> size        : 415, 401, 4  (nrow, ncol, nlyr) #> resolution  : 24.93766, 24.93976  (x, y) #> extent      : 697602.7, 707602.7, 7032171, 7042521  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) #> coord. ref. : RGF93 v1 / Lambert-93 (EPSG:2154) #> source(s)   : memory #> varnames    : ground_concentration_cd_compressed #>               ground_concentration_cd_compressed #>               ground_concentration_cd_compressed #>               ground_concentration_cd_compressed #> names       : sol, plante, herbivore, carnivore #> min values  :   0,      0,         0,         0 #> max values  :   1,      1,        10,         9

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Les animaux ne sont pas statiques. L’exposition d’un individu dépend de ses déplacements (son rayon de recherche de nourriture, sa dispersion). spacemodR permet de simuler ces mouvements, par exemple via des noyaux de convolution (kernels) ou la théorie des circuits (Omniscape).
code: # Calcul des noyaux de dispersion en fonction d'un rayon de mobilité (ex: en pixels) k_herb <- compute_kernel(radius=50, GSD=25, size_std=0.5) k_carn <- compute_kernel(radius=150, GSD=25, size_std=0.5)  # Application de la dispersion sur le spacemodel spcmdl_dispersal <- spcmdl |>   dispersal("herbivore", method="convolution", method_option=list(kernel=k_herb)) |>   dispersal("carnivore", method="convolution", method_option=list(kernel=k_carn))  # Note : le sol et les plantes sont évidemment statiques et ne dispersent pas.

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Maintenant que le système est en place, nous pouvons “injecter” la concentration de notre polluant dans le sol, et modéliser sa bioconcentration et sa bioaccumulation jusqu’au sommet de la chaîne alimentaire grâce à la fonction transfer().
code: # 1. On assigne la grille de concentration réelle dans la couche "soil" spcmdl_dispersal[["sol"]][] <- ground_cd  # 2. On définit les équations de transfert (Facteurs de Bioaccumulation / Bioconcentration) fluxes <- flux(spcmdl_dispersal, default = 1) |>   add_flux("soil", "plant",  ~ 10^x / 32) |> # Equation spécifique pour les plantes   add_flux("soil", "herbivore",  0.5) |>     # Facteur simple pour l'herbivore   add_flux("herbivore", "carnivore",  0.8)   # Facteur simple pour le carnivore  # 3. On rassemble nos noyaux de dispersion pour le calcul de l'exposition kernels <- list(sol = NA, plante = NA, herbivore = k_herb, carnivore = k_carn)  # 4. Calcul du transfert global dans l'écosystème spcmdl_transfer <- transfer(spcmdl_dispersal, kernels, fluxes)  # Visualisation de la contamination absorbée par le carnivore color_transfer <- colorRampPalette(c("white", "#A33D0A"))(255) terra::plot(spcmdl_transfer, col=color_transfer)

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: L’étape finale de l’ERA consiste souvent à générer un Indice de Risque (par exemple, le Quotient de Danger ou l’approche Eco-SSL). Cela permet de cartographier les “Hot-Spots” où les seuils de toxicité de référence sont dépassés.
code: # Définition des classes de risque (de "Sûr" à "Risque Très Élevé") breaks_risk <- c(-Inf, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, Inf) cols_risk <- c(   "darkgreen",   # 0 - 0.1 (Pas de risque)   "green",       # 0.1 - 0.5   "lightgreen",  # 0.5 - 1 (Limite)   "yellow",      # 1 - 5 (Risque modéré)   "saddlebrown", # 5 - 10 (Risque fort)   "#4A2C2A"      # > 10 (Risque très sévère) )  # Projection du risque sur la zone d'étude poly_vect <- terra::project(terra::vect(roi_metaleurop), terra::crs(spcmdl_transfer)) rast_crop <- terra::crop(spcmdl_transfer[["herbivore"]], poly_vect) rast_final <- terra::mask(rast_crop, poly_vect)  terra::plot(rast_final,             breaks = breaks_risk,             col = cols_risk,             main = "Cartographie de l'Indice de Risque (Herbivore)")

text: likelihood defined : yi∼𝒩(μi,σ2) y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma^2) μi=β0+β1xi+βcat[x_cati] \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_{\text{cat}}[x\_cat_i]  : β0\beta_0 global intercept. β1\beta_1 slope coefficient continuous variable xx. βcat[x_cati]\beta_{\text{cat}}[x\_cat_i] specific coefficient (effect) associated category observation ii belongs. σ\sigma standard deviation error term (residuals). model specifies weakly informative priors parameters regularize inferences without overly constraining data: Intercept: β0∼𝒩(0,10)\beta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10) Continuous Slope: β1∼𝒩(0,10)\beta_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10) Categorical Coefficients: βcat∼𝒩(0,10)\beta_{\text{cat}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10) KK categories. Error Standard Deviation: σ∼Half-Cauchy(0,5)\sigma \sim \text{Half-Cauchy}(0, 5). σ\sigma constrained strictly positive (real<lower=0> sigma;) , Cauchy prior automatically becomes truncated Half-Cauchy distribution. Based structure likelihood function, model makes following classical linear regression assumptions: Linearity: relationship continuous predictor xx mean response yy strictly linear. Additivity (Interactions): effect continuous variable (xx) categorical variable (xcatx_{cat}) purely additive. slopes assumed identical across categories; intercepts vary (parallel lines model). Normality Errors: residuals (differences observed predicted values) normally distributed. Homoscedasticity (Constant Variance): standard deviation error term, σ\sigma, assumed constant across values xx across KK categories. Independence: observation ii conditionally independent given parameters.

title: Implementing Eco-SSL model
text: solve equation HQ=FIR×(Soil×Ps+Bi)TRVHQ = \frac{FIR \times (Soil \times P_s + B_i)}{TRV}, table integrates several species-specific parameters: Surrogate Receptor Group: column identifies specific bird species chosen EPA represent entire dietary guild within ecosystem. instance, dove models avian herbivores, woodcock models avian insectivores (foraging soil), hawk models avian carnivores. TRV Cadmium (Toxicity Reference Value): maximum safe daily dose Cadmium bird can ingest without experiencing adverse health effects. avian species assessment, TRV set 1.47 mg/kg bw/day. Food Ingestion Rate (FIR): parameter represents total amount food bird consumes daily, normalized body weight (kg dry food per kg body weight). Notice insectivore (woodcock) highest metabolic demand ingestion rate (0.214) compared carnivore (0.0353). Soil Ingestion Proportion Diet (PsP_s): Birds incidentally swallow soil foraging preening. value represents fraction total daily diet made soil. ground-probing woodcock incidentally ingests soil (16.4% 0.164). Concentration Cadmium Biota Type (BiB_i): column provides bioaccumulation regression equations used estimate much Cadmium transfers soil bird’s specific food source (plants, earthworms, mammals). bridges gap environmental contamination dietary exposure. Eco-SSL (Ecological Soil Screening Level): final calculated threshold. represents maximum allowable Cadmium concentration soil (mg/kg dry weight) ensure target bird remains safe (HQ=1HQ = 1). avian insectivore risk, requiring stringent soil limit 0.77 mg/kg, carnivore protected 630 mg/kg.

title: Implementing Eco-SSL model
text: evaluate spatial distribution environmental risk, calculate Hazard Quotient (HQ) target group across landscape. HQ simply ratio environmental exposure safe threshold (HQ = Exposure / Eco-SSL). B input soil concentration layers (x) currently log10log_{10}-scaled, must first back-transform actual, linear values (using 10^x) performing division. keep model setup clean easy update, first define vector containing specific Eco-SSL thresholds group, apply values within flux() function configure spacemodel object. easily interpret spatial distribution ecological risks, map calculated Hazard Quotients (HQs) using discrete, threshold-based color scale. HQ value 1 represents regulatory tipping point risk, palette split intentionally: areas threshold represented shades green (safe zones), areas exceeding threshold shift yellow dark brown (action risk zones). excluding baseline soil layer focus strictly ecological receptors, plot entire study area subsequently crop mask layers specific Metaleurop Region Interest (ROI) clean, site-focused evaluation.
code: # Define the Eco-SSL thresholds (in mg/kg) for each group in a named vector ecossl_vals <- c(   plant      = 32,   invert     = 140,   mamHerb    = 73,   mamInsect  = 0.36,   birdInsect = 0.77 )  # Build the Eco-SSL thresholds by transforming the log10 soil (10^x)  # and dividing by the specific Eco-SSL value to get the HQ ecossl_threshold <- flux(spcmdl_ecossl_h, default = 1, normalize = FALSE) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "plant", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["plant"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "invert", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["invert"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "mamHerb", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["mamHerb"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "mamInsect", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["mamInsect"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "birdInsect", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["birdInsect"])  # Apply the transfer to compute the spatial risk layers spcmdl_ecossl_risk <- transfer(   spcmdl_ecossl_h,   ecossl_kernels,   ecossl_threshold,   exposure_weighting="potential" ) # Risk colors breaks_risk <- c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, Inf) cols_risk <- c(   "darkgreen",   # 0 - 0.1   "green",       # 0.1 - 0.5   "lightgreen",  # 0.5 - 1   "yellow",      # 1 - 5   "saddlebrown", # 5 - 10   "#4A2C2A"      # > 10 )  names_keep <- names(spcmdl_ecossl_risk)[names(spcmdl_ecossl_risk) != "soil"] spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub <- spcmdl_ecossl_risk[[names_keep]]  terra::plot(spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub,             breaks = breaks_risk,             col = cols_risk) poly <- roi_metaleurop poly_vect <- terra::project(terra::vect(poly), terra::crs(spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub))  rast_crop <- terra::crop(spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub, poly_vect) rast_final <- terra::mask(rast_crop, poly_vect) terra::plot(rast_final,             breaks = breaks_risk,             col = cols_risk)

title: Workflow for Environmental Risk Assessment: Habitat, Food Web, Dispersal, Exposure and Risk
text: package provides complete workflow move raw landscape data risk indices: 1. Habitat Construction: Convert vector shapefiles (e.g., OCS-GE) high-resolution habitat raster grids based species-specific preferences weights. 2. Trophic Web Modeling: Define Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) representing predation herbivory flows across ecosystem. 3. Dispersal & Connectivity: Simulate animal movement flow using advanced dispersal kernels circuit theory (via integration Julia’s Omniscape algorithm). 4. Exposure & Transfer: Calculate Daily Food Intake (DFI) model bioaccumulation transfer contaminants (e.g., Cadmium, Lead, Zinc) food web. 5. Risk Mapping: Generate spatially explicit risk maps (e.g., Eco-SSL indices) identify critical hot-spots ecotoxicological concern.
